Irving grew from 2,615 people in 1950 to more than 100,000 by 1970, and today most of its households rent. Whether you own the house or manage the units, a free call at any hour gets you transferred to an independent Irving-area HVAC firm.

People looking for AC repair in Irving, TX, are as likely to be landlords and renters as homeowners. The Census Bureau puts Irving's owner-occupied rate at about 38 percent, so most households here rent. That changes who is responsible for a broken system, who should place the call, and which city office to contact when a repair drags on. Here is how it works in Irving, and where the free line fits.

Dallas Air & Heating is a phone line, not a repair company. Ring (469) 649-7066 day or night. After an automated assistant takes down the details, it transfers you to an independent HVAC firm covering Irving, which handles the diagnosis and the quote and collects payment from whoever hired it.

Irving: from a 1903 lot sale to Las Colinas

Irving started with a lot auction on 80 acres of ranch land in December 1903 and incorporated in 1914. It stayed a small farm community until after World War II. Then it grew faster than almost anywhere in Dallas County: 2,615 residents in 1950, 45,895 in 1960 and 100,996 in 1970, according to the Texas State Historical Association. The Dallas Cowboys moved to Texas Stadium in Irving in 1971, and the stadium was demolished in 2010.

The 1970s also brought DFW International Airport along the city's western edge and the start of Las Colinas, a planned community on the north side that now covers more than 12,000 acres of offices, apartments and homes around Lake Carolyn. Valley Ranch followed as another master-planned area. The 2020 census counted 256,684 people across about 67 square miles. So an Irving AC call might come from a 1960s house in south Irving, a 1990s two-story near Valley Ranch, or a high-rise apartment in Las Colinas.

Who should make the call in Irving?

The answer depends on who owns the equipment. Here is the usual split.

You own the home

You hire the HVAC company and pay it. Call the line, describe the problem, and you are put through to an independent company that serves Irving.

You rent

Report the problem to your landlord or manager in writing. Irving tells tenants to go to management first, then to Code Enforcement at (972) 721-4829 if it is not resolved.

You are the landlord

Texas law expects diligent repair of conditions that affect a tenant's health or safety once you have notice. The line can connect you with a local company any hour.

What Irving's rental rules mean for a broken AC

Irving inspects its apartment complexes on a schedule. The city says multifamily properties are inspected at least once a year depending on their risk rating, and the highest-risk properties at least twice. Tenants with an unresolved maintenance problem are told to put it in writing to management, let inspectors into the unit to document it, and avoid filing anonymously, because anonymous complaints are hard to act on.

State law sets the larger frame. Under the Texas Property Code, a landlord must make a diligent effort to repair a condition that materially affects the health or safety of an ordinary tenant, once the tenant gives notice and is current on rent. The code mentions cooling directly in one place: when a landlord has agreed to provide heating or cooling equipment, the equipment is producing inadequate heat or cooled air, and a local housing, building or health official has notified the landlord in writing, the tenant gains additional repair remedies. Legal aid groups can explain the details for a specific situation.

For owners and landlords, the practical takeaway is to keep records. Write down when a problem was reported, when the company came out and what it found. A short written diagnosis from the HVAC company is useful for a tenant, a property manager and an insurance claim alike.

So many housing units, so many kinds of equipment

Census Reporter, using the Census Bureau's 2024 American Community Survey, counts roughly 103,500 housing units in Irving, more than in Garland or Mesquite. They range from single-story houses with a furnace in the garage, to townhomes with a closet air handler, to apartment towers with central plant equipment managed by building engineers. A good technician asks what kind of building you are in before guessing at the problem, because a stuck damper in a mid-rise and a dead capacitor on a house can look the same from the thermostat.

Permits, power and gas in Irving

In Irving, electrical, mechanical and plumbing work each need their own permit, applied for online through the city's MGO permit portal. Mechanical permits do not need plans. The Inspections Department, at City Hall on West Irving Boulevard, answers at (972) 721-2371. The city makes a point worth repeating: when a contractor signs the permit, it agrees to do the work to code, and if you sign it yourself, you are the one responsible for fixing work that fails inspection. Permits generally expire 180 days after they are issued if work has not started.

Check the license yourself. In Texas, air conditioning and refrigeration contractors are licensed by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR), and the license number belongs on the company's quotes and invoices. Ask for it and look it up with the TDLR license search (opens in a new tab) before work starts. It is also fair to ask for a certificate of insurance.

Irving is in Oncor's delivery area and the retail electric market. Oncor maintains the wires and restores outages, and the provider you chose bills you. Natural gas service comes from Atmos Energy, which lists Irving in its Mid-Tex Division. Neither utility repairs air conditioners or furnaces. Irving's weather record shows why cooling matters here: the highest temperature recorded in the city is 112 degrees, set in 1980.

Before you call: safe checks for an Irving home or unit

  • Thermostat: in Cool mode, set lower than the room, batteries fresh.
  • Breaker: a tripped AC breaker may be reset once. If it trips again, stop.
  • Filter: in apartments the return grille is often in a hallway ceiling or wall. A dirty filter there can freeze the coil.
  • Outdoor unit: on a house, clear leaves and clutter from around it. In an apartment, note which unit is yours if you know.
  • Water: a puddle under the closet unit, or a system that shut itself off when its drain backed up, should be described on the call.

Common questions

My apartment AC is broken in Irving. Who do I call?

Start with your property manager, in writing. The City of Irving tells tenants to report maintenance problems to management first, and if the problem is not resolved, to contact Irving Code Enforcement at (972) 721-4829 or file a complaint online. Under Texas law, once notified, a landlord must make a diligent effort to fix conditions that endanger a tenant's health or safety.

Does Irving require a permit to replace an air conditioner?

Yes. Irving requires a separate mechanical (HVAC) permit, applied for online through the city's MGO permit portal. Plans are not required for a mechanical permit. The city notes that the person who signs for a permit is responsible for the work meeting code, so let the HVAC company sign for it.

Can an Irving homeowner pull their own HVAC permit?

Irving allows owners of homesteaded property to do some work on their own homes, and a homeowner applying for a residential permit must have a homestead exemption on file with the Dallas Central Appraisal District. For an AC replacement done by a company, the company should pull the permit so it is accountable for the result.

Is a dead AC an Oncor problem in Irving?

Only if the whole house is out. Oncor owns the wires and meters in Irving and restores power, while the retail provider you picked sends the bill. If lights and outlets work, reset a tripped AC breaker once and check the thermostat. If it still will not cool, call an HVAC company.

Gas smell inside my Irving place: what's the first step?

Leave right away and do not use switches on the way out. After you are outdoors, contact 911, or Atmos Energy, Irving's gas utility, at 866-322-8667. Wait for Atmos to clear the home before returning. If a carbon monoxide alarm sounds, get everyone out and call 911.
